stemMd: The final sentence of the passage suggests that the author would regard which of the following as the better measure of a canopy programme's success?
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: The number of saplings planted in a given year

options.label: B
options.textMd: The number of separate streets that receive at least one new tree

options.label: C
options.textMd: The share of new trees planted on public land

options.label: D
options.textMd: The canopy still standing many years after the trees were planted

explanationMd:
The final sentence contrasts two targets. One is "measured by trees planted", and it "rewards the ribbon-cutting". The other is "measured by canopy that still exists in twenty years", and it "rewards the maintenance that nobody photographs". The paragraph has just said that survival depends on maintenance and that shade arrives only after fifteen to twenty years, so the author clearly prefers the measure that rewards maintenance: canopy that survives.

**How to check.** Ask which option the author's own criticism would NOT apply to. Counting saplings, public-land plantings or streets reached all reward planting itself, which is what the sentence calls ribbon-cutting.

distractorRationale.a: This is the measure the author criticises: a target counted in trees planted "rewards the ribbon-cutting" rather than the maintenance that makes trees survive.
distractorRationale.c: Planting on public land is what the second paragraph warns about, since it is cheapest and often in the coolest areas. Measuring success by it would reward the very pattern the author criticises.
distractorRationale.b: Counting streets reached is still a count of planting. It would say nothing about whether the trees survive long enough to give shade, which is the author's concern in the final paragraph.

accessibilityText: A question about the passage on urban tree-canopy targets. It asks which measure of success the final sentence suggests the author would prefer. The options are: canopy still standing many years after planting; saplings planted in a year; share of new trees on public land; number of streets receiving at least one new tree.

provenance.notes: Original inference item. Every distractor is a count of planting activity, which the final sentence criticises.
